# Block 4: Context, disclosure and autonomy {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

Two questions decide how far you can trust anything an AI
`r glossary("assistant")` does with your code:

1. **What can it see?** Its answers are only as good as its context, and
   everything it sees has left your machine.
2. **What can it do?** An assistant that advises leaves you as the filter on
   every change. An `r glossary("agent")` that acts removes that filter.

This block covers both, using Claude Code in the terminal. If you use Posit
Assistant instead, the collapsed boxes give the differences.

*⏱ ~33 minutes*


## Part A: What can the assistant see?

| Surface | Example | What it can see | Can it act? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Browser chat | Any chat website | What you paste | No |
| Terminal agent | Claude Code | Project files, and the output of any command it runs | Yes, in your files and shell |
| Session-aware IDE assistant | Posit Assistant in RStudio or Positron | Your live R session (loaded packages, data frames, console history) and project files | Yes, in your session and files |

:::{.callout-note}
**Knowing versus guessing.** An assistant can describe your data confidently
for two quite different reasons: it has been given real information, or it is
recalling patterns from training data. Only the first is reliable.

It has real information when you pasted the output, when it read a file, when
the IDE injected your session, or when it ran code and read the result. It is
guessing when none of those apply. The tells are a well-known dataset you never
mentioned (`mtcars`, `iris`, `penguins`) or column names and values you never
supplied.

Even with context, a model's account of *what it can see* is unreliable. Check
any data-specific claim against the real object.
:::


### Exercise 1: Context decides the answer

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
The same error, three levels of context (10 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**1. Error only.** Open a new browser chat and ask "What does this error
mean?", pasting only this:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
Error in `mutate()`:
ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`.
Caused by error:
! object 'mass_post' not found
```

The answer can only reason from the error text.

**2. Error plus code plus structure.** Open another new chat and paste:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I am running this code:

  voles |>
    mutate(mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g)

and getting:

  Error in `mutate()`:
  ℹ In argument: `mass_change = mass_post - mass_pre_g`.
  Caused by error:
  ! object 'mass_post' not found

The data structure is:

  Rows: 72
  Columns: 6
  $ subject_id          <chr> "V001", "V002", "V003", ...
  $ sex                 <chr> "M", "F", "M", ...
  $ treatment_arm       <chr> "Control", "Control", ...
  $ mass_pre_g          <dbl> 28.3, 27.9, 30.1, ...
  $ mass_post_g         <dbl> 28.5, 28.0, 30.5, ...
  $ metabolic_rate_post <dbl> 13.21, 12.84, 13.55, ...

What is wrong?
```

It should name the missing `_g` suffix.

**3. No paste at all.** Save the failing code in a script in your workshop
repository. Start Claude Code from the repository's root folder, in `default`
mode, and ask only:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Why does the mutate() call in my script fail?
```

Claude Code can open the script and run code to inspect the data. Then ask:
"How do you know the column names?" Compare its answer with what you know it
was given. If it claims to have seen something it could not have seen, you have
found the unreliability described in the callout above.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Load the data in your R session and run the failing code, then ask Posit
Assistant only: "Why did my last command fail?" A session-aware assistant can
read your console history and the data frame without your pasting anything.
:::

::::
:::

The lesson is not that one route is correct. The answer is only as good as the
context, and context reaches the model by more than one route.


### Disclosure: every route out of your machine

Everything an assistant sees is sent to a model provider. Data leave your
machine by four routes:

:::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Four routes by which data leave your machine for the model provider, and which tools use each route"}
::::: {.dia-flow}
::: {.dia-label}
Route 1: what you paste
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-you}
Errors, output and results you paste into a chat or prompt
:::
::: {.dia-arrow}
any tool
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-plain}
Model provider
:::
:::::
::::: {.dia-flow}
::: {.dia-label}
Route 2: files it reads
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-file}
Copilot: the open file. Claude Code and Posit Assistant: the whole project
folder
:::
::: {.dia-arrow}
read
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-plain}
Model provider
:::
:::::
::::: {.dia-flow}
::: {.dia-label}
Route 3: session context the IDE injects
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-file}
Your live R session: data frames, loaded packages, console history
:::
::: {.dia-arrow}
Posit Assistant only
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-plain}
Model provider
:::
:::::
::::: {.dia-flow}
::: {.dia-label}
Route 4: output of commands it runs
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-ai}
The agent runs `print(voles)` or `head data.csv`
:::
::: {.dia-arrow}
Claude Code, Posit Assistant
:::
::: {.dia-node .dia-plain}
Model provider
:::
:::::
::: {.dia-caption}
Everything on the left of an arrow reaches the model provider. Know which
routes your tool can use before you decide what to show it.
:::
::::::

1. **What you paste.** Errors, outputs, printed results.
2. **Files it reads.** A data file in the repository or project folder.
3. **Session context the IDE injects.** Posit Assistant reads loaded packages,
   data frames and console history, so a data frame in memory can reach the
   model without any paste.
4. **Output of commands it runs.** If an agent runs `print(voles)` or
   `head data.csv`, those values enter its context.

Before you decide what to show, know what the surface can already reach. A data
file committed to the repository, or a tibble loaded in your session, may
already be disclosed.

When you describe a data frame deliberately, three commands reveal increasing
amounts:

- `names(voles)` lists column names only, in their original order.
- `summary(voles)` adds ranges, quartiles and missing-value counts for numeric
  columns: the shape of the data, not individual records.
- `glimpse(voles)` or `str(voles)` adds the first few actual values of every
  column.

:::{.callout-important}
**Before using an assistant on research data**, check three things: whether
your institution permits sending this kind of data to this provider; whether
your ethics approval and data-sharing agreements allow it; and whether a
synthetic or anonymised copy would serve instead. Tool settings that restrict
reading (see [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)) reduce accidental exposure,
but they do not make an agent safe for confidential data: any command it runs
that prints data sends that data to the provider.

For personal or confidential data, let the agent work on a synthetic copy and
run the final code on the real data yourself, outside the agent's workspace.
Hooks and project settings are also code that runs on your machine, and a
cloned repository can carry its own; trust only repositories whose
configuration you have read.
:::


### Context you hold in your head

:::{.callout-note}
## Instructor demonstration (3 minutes)

A data file can supply column names and types, but not your scientific
question or your design intent. Your instructor will ask a new browser chat
this:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
```

and then, in another new chat, this:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
```

The first returns a tour of options (paired tests, change scores, ANCOVA,
mixed models); the second can return a recommendation, because the design and
the question now exist outside your head. Treat even the better answer as a
proposal to check against a statistics text or a colleague. Choosing the
primary analysis is your decision, not the assistant's.
:::


## Part B: What can the assistant do?

The model is the same at every level below. What changes is its
`r glossary("permission mode")`: what it is allowed to do without asking, and
therefore where you sit in the loop. Each level is a `r glossary("rung")` on an
autonomy ladder.

| Rung | What happens | Claude Code | Posit Assistant |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Suggest | Completes the line you are typing | — | Next Edit Suggestions |
| 1. Ask | Answers; changes nothing | Ask a question in `plan` mode | Ask mode |
| 2. Plan | Proposes steps; changes nothing until you approve | `plan` mode | `/plan` |
| 3. Act, with approval | Edits files and runs commands, asking first | `default` mode | Normal mode |
| 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Some actions without asking | `acceptEdits` mode | Auto mode |
| 5. Act, unsupervised | No prompts | `bypassPermissions` | YOLO mode |

In Claude Code, rungs 1 and 2 both use `plan` mode; they differ only in what you
ask for, an answer or a plan. Rung 6, acting remotely on a branch and returning
a pull request, is covered in *Going further* below.

In Claude Code, `Shift+Tab` cycles `default`, `acceptEdits` and `plan`; the
[Claude Code quick reference](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd#cc-quick-reference)
in Block 1 lists the other commands you need. In Posit Assistant, `/plan`,
`/auto`, `/yolo` and `/restricted` switch modes. Use rungs 0 to 3 throughout
this course. Do not use rung 5.

:::{.callout-warning}
**Read the rung's small print.** `acceptEdits` in Claude Code approves more than
edits: it also auto-approves common file commands such as `mkdir`, `touch`, `mv`
and `cp`. A `cp` that overwrites a raw data file needs no approval in that mode.
Posit Assistant's auto mode replaces your judgement with a classifier model's.
Each step up the ladder removes a moment when you would have seen the action
before it happened.

**Approval fatigue is real.** At rung 3, an approval prompt you click through
without reading is rung 5 with extra steps. [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)
covers the rules that hold however tired you are.
:::

Higher rungs make instruction files matter more. At rung 1, a convention the
assistant does not know costs you a re-read. From rung 3 upwards, the agent
acts on its guess, and the guess lands in your files. That is why
[Block 5](11e-instructions-skills.qmd), on instructions and skills, comes next,
and why [Block 6](11f-enforced-controls.qmd), on enforced controls, follows it.


### Exercise 2: The same task, rising autonomy

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

Use your workshop repository, **committed and clean**, so every change is a diff
you can inspect or revert. Never run an agent with uncommitted work you are not
prepared to lose.

**1. Ask.** Start Claude Code in `plan` mode.

**In the terminal:**

```bash
claude --permission-mode plan
```

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
In scripts/explore_voles.R, how would I add a column mass_change equal to
mass_post_g minus mass_pre_g?
```

Read the answer. Confirm with `git status` that nothing changed.

**2. Plan.** Still in `plan` mode, give a goal that spans several files:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a derived mass_change column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g), create a new script scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R
that plots mass_change by treatment_arm, and check that both scripts run
from a fresh R session.
```

Before approving, check that the plan names every file it will touch, does not
touch raw data, says where the plot script goes, and says how it will check the
scripts run. Amend the plan in conversation if any of that is missing.

**3. Act, with approval.** When Claude Code asks whether to proceed, choose
**Yes, manually approve edits**, so it stays in `default` mode and asks before
each edit or command. Read each approval prompt before answering it. Refuse at
least one action you consider out of scope, and note how the agent responds.

**4. Review.** When it finishes, look at what changed:

**In the terminal:**

```bash
git status
git diff
```

Read the diff as you would a colleague's contribution. The agent's statement
that the scripts "still run" is a claim; run them yourself to check it, in the
fresh R session that `Rscript` starts:

**In the terminal:**

```bash
Rscript scripts/explore_voles.R
Rscript scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R
```

**5. Compare.** At which rung did you decide the most? At which rung would you
have missed an unwanted change if you had not read the diff?

**Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you
automate this again?

**6. Start your AI-use log.** Create `docs/ai-log.md` and write the first line
of your `r glossary("AI-use log")` yourself, rather than asking the agent, in
the form set out in Block 1. For example:

```text
2026-10-19; Claude Code (model as shown above the Claude Code prompt); added
mass_change and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff; rejected one
out-of-scope edit.
```

Commit it with the agent's changes. You will add a line after each block in
which an agent does work.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Using Posit Assistant

Use Ask mode for step 1, `/plan` for step 2, and Normal mode for step 3. The
review in step 4 is the same: `git status` and `git diff` in the terminal.
:::

::::
:::


:::{.callout-note}
**Access and cost.** Plans and prices change; check before the session.

- **Claude Code** needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an
  API key; see Anthropic's documentation for current options.
- **Posit Assistant** uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an
  Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant's
  settings.
- **GitHub Copilot** bills in AI credits; check GitHub's plans page for what
  your plan includes.
- **Your institution** may have approved some of these tools and not others.
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **Check:** `git status` and `git diff` after every agent action; the agent's
  report that something "still runs" is a claim until you run it.
- **Reproduce:** work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change
  is a diff you can inspect or revert.
- **Record:** your AI-use log starts here, in `docs/ai-log.md`.
:::


## Check your understanding

**You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it
know them?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "It cannot; it must be guessing",
  answer = "It read a file in your project or ran code that printed the data, and that output entered its context",
  "It can see every file on your computer",
  "It remembers your data from a previous conversation"
))`

**In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Nothing; acceptEdits only changes how diffs are displayed",
  "Only edits to files you have named",
  answer = "It edits files and runs common file commands such as cp and mv without asking, but still asks before other shell commands",
  "Everything, including all shell commands"
))`

**Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The agent's own report that the task succeeded",
  "The approval prompts you saw while it worked",
  answer = "Inspecting the changes with git status and git diff, and running the code yourself",
  "The plan the agent proposed before starting"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

### GitHub Copilot and the remote rung

GitHub Copilot offers the same ladder in its own surfaces. Copilot Chat on
github.com can also see files in the repository you open it from.

| Rung | GitHub Copilot |
|---|---|
| 0. Suggest | Inline suggestions |
| 1. Ask | Ask in Chat |
| 2. Plan | Plan mode in the IDE |
| 3. Act, with approval | Agent mode, approving each tool call |
| 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Agent mode with auto-approval |
| 5. Act, unsupervised | — |
| 6. Act remotely | Cloud agent |

Rung 6, the **Copilot cloud agent**, works on the repository on GitHub, in an
environment GitHub runs. It takes a task such as an issue, works on its own
branch and returns a pull request. Copilot Free includes only limited agent
features; check GitHub's plans page to see whether your plan includes the cloud
agent. The cloud agent appears in the *Going further* section of
[Block 9](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), where its pull request meets a review
gate.
